summary: Defines the core YANG data model for managing a router's routing subsystem, including routes, routing tables (RIBs) and control-plane protocol instances. It is a framework that other YANG modules extend for specific routing protocols. Replaced by RFC 8349.

eli5.summary: A router needs a standard form to fill in, so tools can set it up the same way on any brand. This is that form for the basics of how a router chooses paths.

subtitle: Standard YANG modules for configuring and managing router routing subsystems.

tldr.problem: Routers from different vendors have proprietary ways to configure routing, making it hard to manage networks with mixed equipment and to write standard management tools.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8022 defines a set of YANG modules that provide a common, standard data model for configuring and querying the routing subsystem of a router. It covers routes, Routing Information Bases (RIBs), and control-plane protocols.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now use the same configuration and management tools across routers from different vendors. RFC 8349 later updated the model with additional features and refinements.

facts.label: Minimum implementation
facts.value: Static routing on a simple router

today: RFC 8022 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 8349, which refines and extends the core routing data model with additional features and protocol support.

sections.title: A Standard Form for Routing Configuration
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language designed to represent configuration and state data on network devices. RFC 8022 defines three YANG modules that together form the core routing data model:

  • ietf-routing: The main module that provides generic components of a routing system.
  • ietf-ipv4-unicast-routing: Augments ietf-routing with IPv4-specific data.
  • ietf-ipv6-unicast-routing: Augments ietf-routing with IPv6-specific data and includes a submodule for IPv6 router advertisements.

These modules serve as a framework and foundation. Other YANG modules can extend them to define models for specific routing protocols (like BGP or OSPF) or advanced features like multicast routing or policy routing. A simple static-routing router can be fully configured with just these core modules, while complex routers can augment them with additional protocol-specific models.
sections.eli5: This is the basic form every router understands. Vendors can add extra sections for their own features, but everyone starts with this same basic shape.

sections.title: Routes, RIBs, and Protocols
sections.content:
The core routing data model centers on three building blocks:

Routes: A route is the most basic piece of routing information. It includes a destination prefix (the set of IP addresses the route covers), a route preference (also called administrative distance, used to prefer one route over another), and next-hop information (where to send packets: an outgoing interface, a next-hop IP address, or a special action).

Routing Information Bases (RIBs): A RIB is a list of routes for a particular address family (IPv4, IPv6, etc.). Every router maintains one or more RIBs. For each address family, exactly one RIB is marked as the default RIB where control-plane protocols place their routes by default. Complex routers can have multiple RIBs per address family for policy routing or other advanced purposes.

Control-Plane Protocols: A control-plane protocol is a routing process that populates a RIB with routes. The model defines two pseudo-protocols: direct (routes to directly connected networks, created by the OS from interface configuration) and static (manually configured routes). Real routing protocols like BGP or OSPF are defined in separate YANG modules that augment this core model.
sections.eli5: A route tells the router where to send data. A RIB holds many routes. A protocol fills the RIB with routes. Direct links are automatic, static routes are manual.

sections.title: Configuration and State Data
sections.content:
The model distinguishes between configuration data (what an operator wants the router to do) and state data (what the router currently has running). Configuration data is read-write; state data is read-only.

The configuration hierarchy includes:

  • /routing: Contains the router ID, control-plane protocol instances, and configured RIBs.
  • /routing/control-plane-protocols: Lists instances of routing protocols and pseudo-protocols.
  • /routing/control-plane-protocols/*/static-routes: Where static routes are manually configured.
  • /routing/ribs: Where RIB entries can be defined for advanced uses.

The state hierarchy mirrors the configuration but also includes operational data:

  • /routing-state: Contains the actual router ID in use, interfaces, control-plane protocol status, and actual RIB contents.
  • /routing-state/ribs/rib/routes: The actual routes the router knows about.

Some list entries are system-controlled: the router creates them automatically (like the default IPv4 and IPv6 RIBs). Others are user-controlled: an operator creates them via configuration. Deleting a user-controlled entry removes it from state; deleting a system-controlled entry removes only the operator's configuration for it, leaving the system entry in place.
sections.eli5: Configuration is what you set up; state is what actually happened. The router auto-creates some things, but you can add more. Deleting a user entry removes it; deleting a system entry keeps the system entry but removes your customization.

sections.title: How Other Protocols Extend the Model
sections.content:
The core routing model is designed to be extended. When a new routing protocol (like RIP, BGP, or OSPF) needs a YANG model, the new module follows a pattern:

  1. Define a new identity derived from rt:control-plane-protocol to identify the protocol.
  2. Define protocol-specific route attributes and augment the route definitions under /routing-state/ribs/rib/routes/route with these attributes.
  3. Define configuration parameters for the protocol and augment /routing and /routing-state with protocol-specific data.
  4. Use YANG when statements to make protocol-specific data conditional on the control-plane protocol type.
  5. Optionally encapsulate protocol data in a container with presence to allow mandatory data nodes within the augment.

The RFC provides an example of how this works for the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) in its appendices. This extensibility pattern allows the core model to remain stable while new protocols are added without modification to the core modules.
sections.eli5: When a new routing protocol needs a YANG model, it adds its own data to the core model in a standard way. The core stays the same; the new protocol just plugs in.

sections.title: IPv6 Router Advertisements
sections.content:
The ietf-ipv6-unicast-routing module includes a submodule called ietf-ipv6-router-advertisements that augments the interface and IP configuration modules with IPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) parameters as required by RFC 4861.

These parameters include:

  • send-advertisements: Enable or disable RA sending.
  • max-rtr-adv-interval, min-rtr-adv-interval: How often to send RAs.
  • managed-flag, other-config-flag: Directives for host configuration.
  • link-mtu, reachable-time, retrans-timer: Link characteristics.
  • cur-hop-limit, default-lifetime: Router and route parameters.
  • prefix-list: A list of prefixes to advertise, each with valid-lifetime, preferred-lifetime, on-link-flag, and autonomous-flag.

The RFC clarifies that RFC 4861 allowed implementations to decrement these lifetimes in real time, but modern implementations keep them constant. This model adopts the constant-lifetime behavior, which simplifies implementation and avoids issues with configuration reloads.
sections.eli5: IPv6 routers send periodic announcements to hosts telling them about available networks. This submodule lets you configure all those announcement settings.
